articles.title: ‘Special 26’ in Mumbai: Sacked driver teams up with I-T officials to target ex-employer in fake raid
articles.summary: MUMBAI: In a Akshay Kumar-starrer  Special 26-style plot, a sacked driver allegedly teamed up with two Income Tax officials and others to conduct a fa.
articles.body: MUMBAI: In a Akshay Kumar-starrer Special 26-style plot, a sacked driver allegedly teamed up with two Income Tax officials and others to conduct a fake raid at his former employer’s office in Mumbai and demand Rs 1 crore. The extortion bid was foiled after the company owner asked the alleged raiding team to produce authorisation documents.Andheri police have arrested 10 people in connection with the July 17 incident, including two serving I-T officials. Police said the operation was masterminded by former company driver Santosh Khopatkar, 37, who was sacked about three months before the alleged raid and wanted revenge against his former employer.The fake raid was conducted at Two M Ophthotronics Pvt Ltd in Sahar Cargo Estate, Chakala. Police registered an FIR on September 4 following a complaint by company owner Rajkumar Kandasami.Kandasami told police that his employees called him saying I-T officials had raided the office. Two men in plain clothes later approached Kandasami and his wife near their home, introduced themselves as I-T officials and displayed an identity card. They allegedly forced the couple into an aggregator cab and took them to the office.Sub-inspector Rohan Surve said the accused questioned employees, examined company documents and took away the mobile phones of Kandasami, his wife and staff. They allegedly produced a purported search warrant and obtained Kandasami’s signature on it.The group questioned Kandasami about cash transactions, threatened him with a substantial penalty and offered to settle the purported tax case for Rs 1 crore. However, Kandasami asked them to produce authorisation documents for the raid. The alleged raiding team could not produce any and left empty-handed after around three hours.Kandasami subsequently checked with his chartered accountant and found that the Income Tax department had not ordered any raid at his company.Police said their investigation revealed that Khopatkar had provided the tip-off about the company. He had allegedly approached the I-T officials for help in raiding his former employer after being sacked.The two I-T officials arrested in the case are inspector Sureshkumar Mishra, 57, posted at the Piramal Chamber office in Lalbaug, and tax assistant Sunil Gore, 59, posted at the Kautilya Bhavan office in BKC.Police said Mishra and Gore had allegedly conducted a similar raid on a company in Manpada and demanded Rs 65 lakh.Those arrested earlier in the Chakala case include Khopatkar, Vinay More, 37, Prem Sabnani, 50, Pragnya M, Reshma Shyamrao Warang, 41, and Shabina Shaikh, 48.DCP (West Zone-3) Datta Nalawade said police also took custody of Jitendra More of Thane and Ashok Shinde of Vile Parle West on Thursday. The two were already in judicial custody in connection with the Manpada case.A team led by senior inspector Umesh Machindar, inspector Atul Nikam, assistant inspector Ramdas Kadam and sub-inspectors Rohan Surve and Rameshwar Karpe analysed call records, mobile numbers, dump data, location details and CCTV footage from government and private cameras.Investigators are examining the seized phones for calls, chats, WhatsApp messages and financial transactions to establish the alleged conspiracy, identify other associates and determine the role of each accused.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Anime reaction YouTubers are at war with copyright enforcers
articles.summary: Content creators who repurpose popular IP in their videos say they’re being targeted by copyright trolls.
articles.body: On September 6th, YouTuber Nicholas Light posted a video to one of his channels that made it seem like all of his content was about to be removed from the platform. In the video — ominously titled “My Channel will be Deleted Today” — Light alleges that he was on the receiving end of some of the “thousands upon thousands of false copyright strikes” recently initiated by a company called Remove Your Media. Light spends much of the 13-minute video accusing Remove Your Media CEO Eric Green of being a troll who systematically targets creators whose content mentions or features clips of popular anime series like Bleach and One Piece. It’s not clear how many of Light’s 1.3 million subscribers made it to the end of the video where he admits that YouTube already removed the copyright strikes against his account and informed him that his channel would not be deleted. But in a follow-up video titled “My Channel will NOT be deleted” posted on September 8th, Light thanked himself and “every single person that contributed” to the ongoing conversation about Remove Your Media unfairly threatening creators’ livelihoods. [Media: When I recently spoke with Light via email, he told me that over 60 of his videos had been temporarily taken down after he was hit with over a dozen copyright strikes stemming from Remove Your Media’s Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) takedown requests. Light said that “having a video taken down or struck is almost second nature” for people running reaction channels. But he insisted that the way Remove Your Media has been going after creators is abusive and unrelated to any legitimate interest in protecting copyrighted IP. “I think [Remove Your Media is] trying to get the attention of these companies, to hopefully get hired by them,” Light said. “But because they’re so sloppy, they’re damaging themselves. With all the major channels covering this, they’re doomed.” While it’s easy to get the sense that Light might have been playing up some of this drama for viewers’ attention, it is clear that a number of other content creators have similarly been hit with an inordinate amount of copyright strikes. Many of these creators specialize in anime and gaming reaction videos that feature blurred-out or otherwise altered pieces of copyrighted footage. The creators superimpose the altered copyrighted footage (like anime opening sequences or full episodes) onto videos of themselves reacting to and/or commenting on it. Though these types of videos are kind of like an inverse Mystery Science Theater 3000 where the on-camera creators are meant to be the focus, viewers can also use them as a (less-than-ideal) way to watch copyrighted material without having to pay for it. The creators insist that their content is fundamentally transformative and protected by fair use, but that has not kept YouTube from sending them warnings about their accounts potentially being erased. Remove Your Media legal representative Evan F. Stone told me that Viz Media and Crunchyroll are two of the company’s “biggest anime clients.” Stone explained that Remove Your Media “reports thousands of allegedly infringing links every day” — some of which are “forwarded by the copyright owners themselves,” while others are discovered through online searches. Stone also noted that some clients are “very lenient” with certain types of content, despite their weak fair use defense. But he was adamant that the content being produced by YouTubers Remove Your Media has gone after is not transformative enough to fall under fair use. “Commentary, in this context, does not make the use transformative: these videos show the copyrighted work in its entirety, and a great deal of this content sits behind a paywall,” Stone said. “Add the fact that some viewers are watching these versions rather than the licensed versions, and the effect on the marketplace is real.” Stone also pointed out that some reaction video creators use their free YouTube channels as a way to encourage viewers to subscribe to their paid Patreon pages. In Remove Your Media’s view, when a reaction creator’s business model “is recording someone watching full episodes and selling those recordings, episode included, behind a Patreon paywall,” the company does not need to extensively review every single one of their uploads to file DMCA takedowns in good faith. “For any particular video a creator believes was noticed in error, the counter-notice exists for exactly that situation, and it works,” Stone said. “What [Remove Your Media] is seeing instead is channels countering every single video, full episode uploads included, swearing under penalty of perjury that each one was removed by mistake.” From Light’s perspective, channels like his are producing a unique kind of entertainment that also benefits copyright holders. “It’s free promotion for them at the end of the day,” he explains. Reaction videos of all genres have been popular on the internet for years, and it’s clear from view counts on YouTube that anime fans in particular are watching this kind of content. Light feels that because “the [anime industry] doesn’t do the best job promoting their works outside of Japan,” he and his peers have been picking up the advertising slack with their videos. And while Remove Your Media says that it works on behalf of certain anime distribution platforms including Crunchyroll and Viz Media, Light believes that “no company in the industry would want to align with a company so sloppy.” Crunchyroll did not respond to The Verge’s questions about whether it has hired Remove Your Media to enforce copyright and Viz Media would not comment on record. Similar to Light, Ron and Michelle Jackson — the couple behind the Rice & Ginger YouTube channel — uploaded a video last week announcing that their account might be deleted within a few days after being flagged hundreds of times for copyright violations. In addition to emphasizing that their video was not meant to be clickbait-y, the Jacksons encouraged viewers to subscribe to their Patreon page, and they said that the larger wave of creator takedowns is being caused by “one individual making hell for basically all of us.” The Jacksons did not respond to The Verge’s ask for comment about whether that unnamed individual might be Eric Green or Remove Your Media and how they were able to avoid having their channel deleted on the date (September 6th) listed in their first video addressing the situation. On September 9th, the YouTubers said that their account was now scheduled to be deleted the following day, and they described YouTube’s approach to enforcing copyright as a broken system that allows for AI-powered mass reporting. By September 10th, the Rice & Ginger YouTube channel was still online, and the Jacksons were back with a new video thanking Light for speaking out on their behalf and “saving” their channel. [Media: When I reached out to YouTube asking how it handles DMCA takedown disputes between reaction video creators and IP rightsholders, policy communications manager Jack Malon said that the company “does not decide who owns the rights to content.” Rather than mediating the legality of who owns the copyrighted content and whether a creator’s videos fall under fair use, YouTube brings the two parties together and leaves it to them to work the matter out between themselves. “When we receive valid legal requests, we remove the content to comply with copyright law,” Malon said. “If uploaders believe they have the right to use the material, including for exceptions like fair use, they can file a counter notification.” Malon added that YouTube only removes creators’ videos “when a rightsholder submits a valid and legal takedown request” because the company has to comply with copyright law. According to YouTube, creators can solve copyright strikes by submitting counter notifications — a process that involves providing evidence of ownership or permission to use all elements featured in the removed content. In response to my questions about how Remove Your Media selected the creators that were affected by the takedowns, he said that the company prioritized going after YouTube channels that generate “feeder traffic for paywalled copies of episodes nobody licensed to them.” “For any particular video a creator believes was noticed in error, the counter-notice exists for exactly that situation, and it works,” Stone said. “What [Remove Your Media] is seeing instead is channels countering every single video, full episode uploads included, swearing under penalty of perjury that each one was removed by mistake.” Malon told me that, after a creator submits counter notifications, their videos can be restored and the strikes on their accounts can be resolved “if the rightsholder does not respond with proof of legal action to restrain the allegedly infringing content.” But it’s not entirely clear how YouTube confirms the validity of a claimant’s purported ownership of removed content. On September 10th, Light returned to his channel with another video lambasting both Remove Your Media and YouTube for the way the companies have gone about initiating and handling DMCA disputes. Light said that the Jacksons’ videos will be restored within 10 business days as a result of “all of the noise that [we] made together,” and he addressed people who have speculated that he might be leaning into this drama for financial gain. “It’s funny to me I start having problems with my AdSense the 10 days I choose to go after YouTube,” Light said, explaining that his videos have been demonetized during the DMCA fight. “Really makes you think. So maybe we should shut the fuck up when we say stupid shit like ‘he’s banking on the situation. He’s only doing this for money.’” Though Light and others who have spoken out about the way YouTube handles copyright issues might not be trying to capitalize on being deplatformed, this drama has highlighted how certain dynamics of the content creator economy may be changing. Anime reaction videos probably aren’t going away anytime soon, but it does seem like studios and distributors are becoming more aggressive about monitoring how their IP is being repurposed online. And while creators of all kinds still rely on fair use to produce the content that pays their bills, they may need to tread much more carefully if they want to avoid getting caught up in an aggressive purge.

articles.title: Want to quit posts, not Cong; party is my blood & bones: Harish Rawat after ED raid on aide
articles.summary: Harish Rawat says he may quit Congress committee posts, not the party, after ED raids aide Chandan Jeena in UKSSSC 2016 exam case; Rs 1.2cr seized.
articles.body: Dehradun: Former Uttarakhand chief minister and Congress leader Harish Rawat on Saturday expressed his desire to step down as member of the state Congress Working Committee and the All India Congress Committee (AICC) Working Committee following an Enforcement Directorate (ED) raid on the residence of his aide, Chandan Singh Jeena.The ED conducted searches at Jeena’s residence in Dehradun on Thursday in connection with alleged irregularities in the Uttarakhand Subordinate Service Selection Commission’s (UKSSSC’s) Gram Panchayat Vikas Adhikari examination in 2016. Jeena is Rawat’s personal assistant and had served as his officer on special duty (OSD) between 2014 and 2017.Speaking to TOI, Rawat clarified that he has neither resigned from the party posts nor was he quitting the party. “Membership of the Congress is in my blood and bones. Whatever I am has been shaped by the party, and I will carry that identity with me till my last breath,” he said.Rawat said he was “considering resigning from the two party posts as a moral responsibility” since the allegations levelled were during his tenure as chief minister. “Such decisions are not taken in haste. Several factors, including party preparations, have to be considered,” he said.He maintained that though Jeena was his OSD, “he was not in a position to influence recruitment examinations”. “Only the chief minister, chief secretary or secretary (personnel) can take a call on recruitment examinations,” the former CM said.In a post on Facebook, Rawat said the ED action at the residence of one of his associates appeared aimed at creating a political narrative ahead of the Uttarakhand elections. He said he was ready to appear before the CBI, ED or income-tax authorities wherever required and respond to any allegations.“Whenever anyone asked me when the election was being held, I would joke that it would be held when the CBI came knocking at my door. If it has not come yet, it means the polls will be held only in March-April next year. But this time, by knocking at the house of one of my associates, an attempt has been made to create a narrative,” he said.Rawat also said that if there had been any lapse in the recruitment process during his tenure, he was willing to accept responsibility. He claimed that more than 42,000 govt posts had been filled during his govt’s three-year tenure and appealed to anyone with evidence of his involvement in irregularities to submit it to the investigating agencies or state police.The ED in its official communication said its searches on Thursday were conducted under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act in connection with alleged irregularities in the UKSSSC’s 2016 Gram Panchayat Vikas Adhikari examination. “The case stems from an FIR registered at the Dehradun vigilance police station and three subsequent FIRs,” it said.According to the agency, Rs 32 lakh in cash, gold coins, 13 gold chains and 12 luxury watches, including Rolex, Rado and Piaget, were recovered during the searches. “Bank accounts belonging to Jeena and his family members, containing a total balance of Rs 52.16 lakh, were also frozen,” the ED stated in a statement.The agency put the total value of the assets seized and frozen at around Rs 1.2 crore. It said Jeena’s mobile phone had been seized for forensic examination and that the value of 12 watches was yet to be assessed.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Adam Conover explains how YouTube ruined everything
articles.summary: Comedian, writer, and YouTuber Adam Conover discusses the media, entertainment, and labor landscape in the age of Google-dominated streaming video.
articles.body: Today, I’m joined by comedian, podcast host, and YouTuber Adam Conover. Adam is a familiar face to anyone who’s spent time on the internet. He got his start, like so many successful comedy writers, at CollegeHumor back in the day. That was before transitioning into cable TV with Adam Ruins Everything, then onto Netflix, and all the way back to YouTube again, where he posts videos and hosts a podcast called Factually! That is exactly the kind of career path that fascinates me, and it also happens to touch on basically every major Decoder theme there is. You’ll hear upfront that Adam does not in fact like the word “creator” — he’s got a unique perspective on it that speaks to how he sees tech platforms and their leverage. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- We get deep into what Adam thinks really happened to the TV business — that Hollywood ceded whole categories of TV programming to YouTube in the chase to become Netflix and HBO. Adam also pushes back on the idea that any of this was democratizing — YouTube, he argues, is in fact a worse gatekeeper than the networks, because you can’t actually argue or negotiate with a recommendation algorithm. I think you’re really going to enjoy this conversation, I know I did. Remember to please subscribe to our YouTube channel for new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: comedian Adam Conover on YouTube, gatekeepers, and the business of making things online. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Adam Conover, you’re a comedian, you’re a podcaster, you’re a YouTuber, you’re a board member on the Writers Guild of America West. I’m sure you have additional titles. Welcome to Decoder. I’m also a standup comic. That’s often how I describe myself, my identity as a comedian. But yeah, thank you so much for having me. I’m a fan of the show. I have so many questions for you about this moment in media and entertainment. You have a view into all of it. Live comedy is a thing that is successful in America in 2026. Sitcoms don’t exist, which is a video I just watched that you made. There’s some disconnect with how we make this stuff, how we distribute the stuff, and how we pay for the stuff. Like I said, you have a view into Hollywood, you have a view into television, a view into YouTube. Let’s just start at the very beginning. I listed off a bunch of things and you said you identify as a standup comic. How many roles do you have? How many things do you do? I’m a standup comic. I’m a comedy writer. I’m a television host. I’m a member leader in the Writers Guild of America. I also now basically run a small business as a YouTube podcaster. I recently hired my first full-time employee to help me do all the things I do, but beyond that, I have a bunch of freelancers. I’m one of many people trying to make my way in this new, massively disrupted media landscape, where the companies that used to make media seem intent on destroying themselves and their businesses, giving up large swaths of the industry to tech giants, which are trying to crush us under their heel. So, it’s an interesting time to be a comedian, to say the least. I’m interested in all that. That dynamic between the tech giants, the people who make content for those platforms, and Hollywood — let’s just call it the Death Star of Hollywood — seems as fraught as ever. I want to start with a really basic question. You describe yourself as a YouTuber and a podcaster. Do you think you’re a creator or an influencer? God! I mean, I don’t like those words. I think a lot of people don’t, but I do use them because that’s the terminology we’ve started to use. I feel the word “creator” was created by the social media companies as a way to trick people into entering an extremely inequitable economic bargain. Basically they promise, “Hey, Mr. Beast makes a billion dollars. You could be Mr. Beast. Why don’t you work for us basically for free for the rest of your life in the hopes that one day, we’ll break off a little chunk of ad revenue for you?” That is what they mean by creator. We used to be writers, performers, talent, Hollywood labor, or media labor. Creator is like when Avon or Mary Kay calls you an entrepreneur. [Laughs] “Oh, you’re an entrepreneur, you’re starting your own business.” Am I? Or is that an illusion that you want me to buy into because it obscures what you have done to the industry I work in? We’re just going to get into it. This is why I wanted you here. So my thesis on Decoder and now increasingly on anyone else’s podcast who will have me, is that the entire entertainment complex — all of Hollywood and now the music industry to some extent — could not acknowledge that their real competition is the army of teenagers who work for free on YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. These platforms really do not pay any money. Instagram will literally pay you no money. TikTok will maybe pay a tiny fraction of a penny for every view that you get. YouTube used to be the gold standard, but it just changed its rules. It is now harder than ever to get started in the YouTube Partner Program and get paid actual money from YouTube. But people cannot stop expressing themselves. They cannot stop themselves from wanting to be Mr. Beast. So, there they are, infinite free content for the tech giants. Warner Bros. Discovery, Disney, and everyone else have to pay Hollywood celebrities to desperately try and get people to come to the movies. And the economic disparity of that simply cannot be acknowledged. Because if you do that and you’re [Disney CEO] Josh D’Amaro or [Warner Bros. Discovery CEO] David Zaslav, you should just put all your money in the S&P 500 and shut it down. I agree with most of that. I think the competition is a bit more fine-grained than that. Obviously, the movies compete with TikTok to the extent that there’s a limited number of minutes in the day, but movies are also competing with literally every other human activity. The movies are competing with you playing soccer in the park with your friends, right? There will always be a market for the high end of entertainment because new media forms never completely replace old ones. They compete with them and take some of their share. People still read novels, people still go to plays, and people still listen to the radio. Old forms of media don’t go away altogether. There’s always still a market for them. The market just gets smaller and a bit more specific. So, I’m not sure about the idea that David Zaslav is competing with TikTok. However, he is very specifically competing with YouTube, because YouTube has specifically gone into the television space and it was doing it for about 10 years before the TV industry noticed at all. People have started to notice over the past year. I have started every single conversation I’ve had in Hollywood over the last two years with, “Did you know that YouTube is the largest streaming service on television sets?” Forget laptops, forget phones. I know you know this, Nilay, but I blow people’s minds with this in Hollywood. What those companies haven’t realized was in their rush to chase Netflix, Netflix came in and disrupted them directly. They said, “We all have to create our own mini HBOs that everyone is going to pay $15 a month for.” Obviously, that’s ludicrous. That was never going to be a workable business model, but that’s what they thought for about five years. In their rush to do that, they destroyed linear television. They destroyed the cable business. You can argue that people prefer to watch when they want, whatever. But what they never figured out how to work on streaming was about 60 percent of television: news, talk shows, comedy talk shows, lifestyle programming, The Drew Barrymore Show, travel shows, the weather. They let all of those things go to YouTube specifically. Now when people are like, “I just want to watch somebody talk about home improvement for a little bit. I want to hear somebody talk about the Knicks. I want to hear a funny person talk about the news,” they go to YouTube first, and it’s all free. YouTube’s entire business model is, “We don’t pay for content. We break off a chunk. If we make a lot of money, you get 50 percent.” That’s better than most of the other revenue share models for ads. But that is the thing I think they still haven’t grappled with. Here’s a good example of this. A couple years ago, I was pitching a game show. I had a huge piece of IP attached. It was, I thought, a good pitch. I went to a streaming service to pitch it, and they said, “Here’s our problem with game shows. We can get people to watch one episode. We can’t get people to watch a whole season in a weekend.” I was like, “Wait, your whole business model doesn’t work if people don’t watch a whole season on the weekend? That’s not how people watch game shows.” So, if you are conceding all of game shows, along with all these other formats, you’re conceding a huge swath of what used to be your business. Now, you are only focused on the very high end. You don’t have all of that cheaper programming anymore. I’m in the Writers Guild as what we call a “comedy variety writer.” I do nonfiction comedy like The Daily Show. The networks literally don’t make that kind of thing anymore. My old show, Adam Ruins Everything, ran for 65 episodes. It was a hit for the network and second-biggest show on TruTV. I could not sell a show anything close to that now because networks are like, “Well, we haven’t figured out how to get people to watch if it’s not like a high-end prestige drama starring Adam Scott.” Well, YouTube has, so people like me have been driven to YouTube with disastrous effects on the media landscape, both on the amount of money that we make but also on the kind of media that gets made. I make a good living. I make as good a living as I did as a TV host. I’m very lucky to do so. But now I have a couple freelancers instead of a room full of writers, cinematographers, actors, all of these funny people who made a really good comedy product. Now when you want to get the comedy news, you don’t get to watch The Daily Show or The Colbert Report. Those shows are going away. You get to watch [Andrew] Schulz riff on the news with his three dumbass friends in front of a curtain for $0. Those shows have $0 budgets. The middle has evaporated. My whole thing in media right now is trying to figure out how to rebuild a bit of the middle. How do I get a little bit of a budget so I can do something a little bit better than a podcast and a little bit closer to a television show? I think there’s still a market for it. It’s just that nobody is serving it currently. That’s really what I want to dig into because I’m very curious how that budget comes back. If I just take what you’re describing — like when you were on truTV or if you made a show for another cable network back in the day like MTV — they had pretty good business models. Everyone in the country would pay their cable bill and MTV would get a piece of that money no matter what. That was really lucrative. Not only could they afford writers’ rooms, cinematographers, people who hire the cameras, all those people could be unionized, demand better wages every year, and all the other stuff that unionized employees can do. They could also afford accountants, healthcare professionals, benefit service people, and highly paid CEOs. A cable channel’s overhead was massive, and maybe it was always all wrong. Maybe that overhead should have always flowed back to the content in some other way, but the business model was lucrative because the distribution was lucrative. We had convinced everyone in America to pay for television. And they sold ads against the shows. My show was in the black. It costs this much to make the show, we sell this many ads, here are the rates we get for the ads, and here’s the money we get from the cable company. The show was in the black. That’s why we ran for five years. Most other shows on television are currently in the black. We have two problems. One, the streamers don’t know how to make a show in the black anymore. They’re like, “We have this many subscribers.” How many people signed up for Apple TV Plus to watch Widows Bay? They do this weird math. That’s the first thing. The second thing — and this is a little bit my own theory — is that they gave up decades of business development in the advertising business. Why was CBS able to get a certain rate for The Late Show with Steven Colbert? Because CBS has been negotiating with Johnson & Johnson for 100 years saying, “Here’s how much a spot on CBS is worth.” You cannot rebuild that in an instant. Netflix tricked the entire industry into thinking there wasn’t going to be any advertising ever again, they all destroyed those businesses, and now they’re trying to rebuild them on Peacock. It’s like they gave up a business model that actually made them money. On the other hand, you’ve got YouTube, which is, of course, a massive advertising business, but it’s completely scrambled. The advertisers that I’m able to get on my show are all direct-to-consumer (DTC) brands. It’s MeUndies or whatever. It’s meal kits, subscription services, stuff like that. A lot of them are great, but where’s Coke and Chevy, you know what I mean? Car commercials used to pay for the media you watched. It was Don Draper shit. They didn’t realize that they were throwing the baby out with the bath water and that all of us have to somehow figure out how to rebuild. I do have a theory for how that might happen on the YouTube end that I’m, unfortunately, currently trying to pursue as a business person because that’s what I have to be now. I think a lot of creators go through this moment where you’re constantly being led along and tempted. Sometimes, you step over the line and you don’t even realize you’ve done it until after you’ve done it. Well, I thought I was behaving with integrity in the moment, but looking back, why would anybody think that I was? Does that mean I really did? I mean, that’s the situation we’re in. I’m happy to say that I fucked up by doing so. I also believe that you make mistakes, you acknowledge it, and you do something corrective, which is what I did my best to do. Luckily, the lion’s share of my audience was like, “Oh, this video was really great. Thank you for the thorough explanation and for eviscerating the product.” That thing is hilarious, by the way. I would encourage people to watch your video and all the other videos. Any coverage of the Orb that isn’t literal sponcon is like, “What are we doing here?” Let me ask you about this. You obviously learned a huge important lesson. If you had worked in a media company or entertainment company of any kind, that would become institutional knowledge. “We screwed up. We’re never going to do this again.” Now, a bunch of people have had this experience, and when new people come in and try to do this thing again, we’re just going to say no. But you have to do that alone. Every creator has to do that alone. Yeah. My joke on the show for ages is that every YouTuber gets their wings when they make the video about how mad they are at YouTube. I’m about to make that video actually. I’ve got it locked and loaded. Finally, you’re going to grow up, Adam. This actually might be it. This is the beginning of it. Well, the reason I ask that is because in the old way, there were unions. You are part of a union. The union and the big Hollywood studios would negotiate. These are repeat players, so even if they were antagonistic, the negotiations were towards a common purpose because you were going to do it again in three years. That created a kind of institutional knowledge, or a set of shared goals at the very least. If the tactics and specific negotiations got heated, at least the goals were the same. No one can do that with YouTube. Ben Smith from Semafor was just on the show and he said that people are building real businesses and real careers on top of YouTube. But YouTube has — probably to its own benefit and to the detriment of the media industry — built a system where it’s for individuals and no one has any leverage except for YouTube. You and I cannot get together and go demand terms from YouTube. If we got a thousand YouTubers together to demand terms from YouTube, it would still laugh. It wouldn’t even take the call. It would say, “There’s another thousand teenagers who will work for free. Good luck.” How do you change that? You have a very unique perspective as someone who has organized against Hollywood. Can you change that for the platforms? If I’m putting my labor organizer hat on, I don’t think the organizing target is YouTube itself. I think it’s the channel. So, I wouldn’t try to organize YouTube. I’d try to organize Mr. Beast’s staff, who — you’ve probably done some reporting on it yourself — are horribly abused and underpaid. That is the reality of the economy. It’s actually not the case that all the biggest YouTubers are individuals. The biggest YouTubers are companies. Go look at Adam Savage. That guy is basically doing a cable show every single day. Go look at Hank Green. I love Hank Green. I look at him and I go, “How many people are helping him to make these videos?” You know what I mean? If you want to do something that’s big, constant, and brings in the money, it is a large scale enterprise. It’s in YouTube’s interest to encourage those big channels to get bigger. Monopolies or consolidation are sort of the law of economics unless you’ve got a strong antitrust to prevent them. I see YouTube getting even bigger, the bigger channels getting even bigger, and them getting big enough to organize. Like you said yourself, you’re The Verge, you are a YouTube channel, and you have a unionized staff. And we’re starting to see that happen in the YouTube space. We’re starting to see the staffs of specific channels unionizing. So, if the top 100 channels do grow big enough, could they go to YouTube and say, “Hey, we demand a better split?” Yeah, they could. Is that going to benefit all the people who work for the channels? Probably not, but it becomes more of a B2B negotiation. You know what it becomes more like? When the cable channels were arguing against Spectrum, Charter, and all of those. They would have those carriage battles and those kinds of wars. It becomes that kind of dispute. So, YouTube is making itself a cable monopoly on top of the internet. I think that’s what the dynamic is. However, the original point of the creator economy was to separate labor from each other and, in fact, make the labor so invisible that even if you’re not doing it professionally, you’re kind of ambiently doing it all the time. When you open YouTube or Instagram, how often are you watching someone do it professionally versus how often are you watching someone do it for fun? Having one video go viral; or making one video a week to promote their dentistry business; or making one video a week because they hope to go pro but they actually never will and Instagram hasn’t told them. That’s the huge dark matter of social media. None of those people will be paid. Those people are truly un-unionizable. Sorry, but what it’ll eventually take is the government making some regulations around this. Where we’re starting to see that is with how different states are treating gig workers like rideshare drivers. You’re starting to see that action happening. There have been battles in California and in other states as well. They’re slow. We’re certainly not close to being all the way there. Again, this looks to me like we’re doing the history of the labor movement again. The capitalists have consolidated. They figured out a new industrial revolution that has impoverished everybody and had us working for penny wages. It’s going to take a lot of people organizing, a lot of labor power, and the government figuring out that there’s a problem to do something about it. It’s going to take decades. Hopefully it won’t take violence in the streets, which is what it took during the late 19th and early 20th centuries as the labor movement worked its way towards labor peace. So often when I think about these things, everyone wants to say, “Oh, it’s new. It’s new. It’s new.” Actually, we’ve gone back to the beginning in so many areas. One of our great reporters, Mia Sato, has a line and a thesis she’s reporting out that influencers are the new gig workers. There’s just a lot of echoes in there. Oh yeah. I want to end by asking about Hollywood. You’ve come out very strongly against the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. There’s an argument in everything you’re describing that we should just let Hollywood kill itself. We should just let David Ellison spend all of his dad’s money buying a studio, running CBS News into the ground. These things are doomed. There’s a version of this where the big fights to stop them from killing themselves so that the writing staff of whatever show on whatever network can persist for a little longer just slows down the apocalypse. You can’t fix it. Do you think it’s fixable, or are you just trying to slow down the apocalypse? First of all, I think all effort that you put into fighting this shit is good effort. Even if the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger happens and it costs them a lot more time and money, well, that’ll make the next monopolist think a little longer about the next monopoly. We are starting to see an epochal shift in antitrust. Even people like [former Federal Trade Commission chair] Lina Khan and [former FTC commissioner] Alvaro Bedoya are doing amazing work out of office. You can imagine if Democrats take power again. Even the Republicans are starting to do antitrust a little bit. So, we are making progress there. The most pernicious lie the tech industry tells is about its own inevitability. “Oh, oopsie! Hey, we just invented something so good that everything you used to like has to die. Oh, sorry, you got to get with the program.” No, these people killed our businesses purposefully with mal intent. The first time this ever happened to me was during the Facebook pivot-to-video era. I used to work at CollegeHumor. We had a great business making videos on the internet. Facebook lied about the traffic that their videos were getting. We pivoted a huge amount of the business to Facebook, and it cratered a huge amount of CollegeHumor’s business. CollegeHumor later became Dropout TV, which is a wonderful media success story that I’m really proud of. But it’s that kind of thing. When you look at this shit, half of it is just Mark Zuckerberg lying to people over and over again. So, we don’t need to accept it as some law of the universe. The last part of it is that I don’t just make this argument because I miss having union health insurance and hanging out with funny people writing stuff. Of course I miss those things. Of course I’m sad about the death of the creative class in Hollywood. I got into this because I like movies. I like television. People still do like movies. Talk to people. They’re not like, “No, I never want to see a movie again.” They’re like, “What happened to the good movies?” Go watch Terminator 2 with anybody, and they’ll go, “I wish I could see a movie like this now. Why won’t they make me this movie anymore?” By the way, the box office is having a really good year because they made a couple good fucking movies this year. Big movies and small movies. You’ve got Obsession and Backrooms. You’ve got The Odyssey. Even the Marvel bullshit has had a pretty good year. So, we still love this art form. The movies are one of America’s greatest cultural legacies. It’s like the movies, jazz, and soul food are America’s three biggest contributions to world culture. We can’t let it die. The fact that this entire art form is very effortful and takes a lot of money doesn’t mean that we should accept a world in which it doesn’t exist because a couple of billionaires wanted to lie and steal from each other. We don’t need to accept that world. We can, in fact, have a world that has room for YouTube and television and the movies and, by the way, plays and novels and all the other art forms that people love. We just have to not let these idiots and assholes destroy their own and each other’s businesses. I can’t think of a better place to end it. Adam, you’re going to have to come back soon. This was incredible. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Nilay, thank you so much for having me. I had a blast. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! Decoder with Nilay Patel A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems. SUBSCRIBE NOW!

articles.title: Netflix is making a Crazy Taxi movie and a Sonic show with ‘edge’
articles.summary: Netflix is teaming up with Sega for three new video game adaptations: Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and Stranger Than Heaven.
articles.body: Netflix has announced three new adaptations of Sega games: a Crazy Taxi film, a Sonic animated series “built for kids who want to feel a little edge,” and a live-action movie based on the upcoming Stranger Than Heaven from Yakuza developer RGG Studio. The Crazy Taxi movie will be the first project released, though it doesn’t have a debut date yet. Netflix also already has three seasons of a Sonic show called Sonic Prime. Here’s Netflix’s descriptions of the upcoming adaptations: Crazy Taxi: > Since its 1999 arcade debut, Crazy Taxi has put players behind the wheel of a fearless cabbie racing the clock through chaotic city streets — flying off ramps, dodging traffic, and chasing tips with punk-rock energy that became the series’ signature. The latest title in the franchise, Crazy Taxi: World Tour, is scheduled for release in 2027. The beloved writing duo behind the 2025 reboot of The Naked Gun, Dan Gregor & Doug Mand, will bring the game’s chaotic, comedic spirit to the adaptation, with Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher, and Toru Nakahara, the visionary producers behind the Sonic franchise, are on board to produce. Sonic: > The new animated series, currently in development with Carlos Stevens and Toru Nakahara, will present Sonic and his friends as heroes for an upper pre-school audience — a high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of “that’s my crew” wish fulfillment. Stranger Than Heaven: > From RGG Studio — developer of the Like a Dragon / Yakuza series — STRANGER THAN HEAVEN takes place in early 20th-century Japan, following a foreigner who claws his way from destitute stranger to feared yakuza to entertainment tycoon. Against the backdrop of a changing nation, how will he build an empire while balancing honor and betrayal? Details are under wraps, but a live-action film will bring a new lens to this epic world and franchise.

articles.title: 2026 Emmys red carpet arrivals: Follow live updates as stars celebrate TV's biggest night
articles.summary: The show, hosted by Mariska Hargitay, will be broadcast live on NBC and livestreamed on Peacock at 8 p.m. ET.
articles.body: TV's biggest night is here! The 2026 Emmy Awards will be presented tonight in Los Angeles, with the stars of critically acclaimed shows vying for the coveted statuettes honoring television's best programs and performances from the past year.The show will be broadcast live on NBC and livestreamed on Peacock at 8 p.m. ET. Mariska Hargitay, longtime star of Law & Order: SVU, will be the first woman to host the ceremony in 15 years.The Pitt leads the way with 25 nominations, followed by Hacks with 24 nods — a record for a comedy series — and newcomers Widow's Bay (19), Pluribus (18), Beef (16) and DTF St. Louis (13).Jason Bateman, star of DTF St. Louis, received two nominations for the HBO dark comedy (one as a performer, one as a producer) and two for the Netflix drama Black Rabbit, in which he starred and which he directed.Other stars with multiple nominations included Matthew Rhys (two for Widow's Bay as a performer and producer, one for The Beast in Me as a performer). Rhys won an Emmy in 2018 for his acting in The Americans. His partner and costar on the show, Keri Russell, could win her first — she's nominated again for The Diplomat. There will be 19 Emmy Awards presented on tonight's primetime telecast. That's in addition to about 100 Creative Arts Emmys that were handed out during a two-night gala earlier this month, with Widow's Bay snagging the most (8), followed by Bad Bunny's Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show (7), and DTF St. Louis and The Traitors (6 each).Hargitay, who won an Emmy in 2006 for her work on Law & Order: SVU, won two for My Mom Jane, the HBO documentary she directed about her mother, Jayne Mansfield.Follow our live blog below for live updates from the show, behind-the-scenes moments, analysis and much more.Photo illustration: Gabriella Turrisi/Yahoo News

articles.title: WWE Raw results, grades (Sept. 14): Roman Reigns retains over Penta in Mexico City thriller
articles.summary: Roman Reigns and Penta tore down Mexico City's Arena CDMX Monday night on "WWE Raw."
articles.body: "WWE Raw" was in Mexico City at Arena CDMX on this Monday, Sept. 14, following AAA TripleMania weekend. After hyping up Roman Reigns' first match on "WWE Raw" since the company moved to Netflix in January 2025, the reigning World Heavyweight Champion and Penta went all out in front of the Mexican crowd.Barn = BurnedIt was never going to happen, but the whole country of Mexico may have erupted had Penta dethroned Reigns for the world title in the main event tonight.This was about as perfect of a main event as you could’ve asked for to close out TKO’s Latin-themed weekend of combat sports. Ever so rarely do we see Reigns compete these days, not only on TV, but in general. And for a match where he was the uber heel against the hometown warrior, this gave off a Hulk Hogan vs. Rock-like vibe.LISTEN TO THIS PLACE 🤯@PENTAELZEROM pic.twitter.com/WmDQCqpevM— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 Roman is in enemy territory tonight! 👀@PENTAELZEROM pic.twitter.com/MqMi17tfg8— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 As amazing as it all was and as much as it delivered, I'll acknowledge right away that it didn't earn a perfect five on the crown scale. That's mostly because of the slow pace the match carried in its start — accompanied by such a deflating ending.Again, Reigns was never going to lose. But his win completely silenced the white-hot Mexico City crowd, as if it transported the entire audience to a random show in Birmingham, Alabama. (Wait, that was last week, wasn't it?)But why couldn't Reigns have lost? The man is truly bulletproof at this stage of his career, and this was one of those times when WWE could easily justify interference, since Reigns is currently tied up in ongoing issues with LA Knight, Solo Sikoa and the 946. Nonetheless, Penta's Springboard Destroyer, in particular, was a real ticket-seller. If there was ever a moment to choose out of the match as the No. 1 highlight, it was that.Reigns taking the Penta Driver also looked pretty incredible.THIS MATCH 🤯@PENTAELZEROM | @WWERomanReigns pic.twitter.com/ckxvolaiDz— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 HOW did @WWERomanReigns kick out of THAT!!! 😲 pic.twitter.com/AqKlydmHIW— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 A SHOW-STOPPING MATCH!!! 🔥@WWERomanReigns defeats Penta and retains the World Heavyweight Title! pic.twitter.com/AFQcVTuInq— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 Moving forward, the door feels like it’s been left open for a revisit to this matchup, purely out of interest in seeing Penta win as an underdog. But those story beats I just mentioned are ever-present, leaving Reigns surely set to collide with either Knight or Sikoa next — either at, or as a result of, Money In the Bank. After "Raw" went off the air, WWE indeed hinted that it’s saving that special moment for one Mr. Knight. (One can hope.)After his successful title defense against @PENTAELZEROM, @WWERomanReigns gets DROPPED by @RealLAKnight 😮🫨😮🫨 #WWERaw pic.twitter.com/4mes2kvHBN— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 Speaking of Money In the Bank…QualifiedWe saw more seeds planted for the Money In the Bank ladder matches tonight. Je'Von Evans defeated Big Cass and Austin Theory to qualify, while Lola Vice made good on her main roster debut, pinning Raquel Rodriguez in their match with NXT's Keilani Jordan.Both winners were decent surprises, especially with Rodriguez holding the Intercontinental title. Vice entering the Money In the Bank match signals an immediate push for her, win or lose. The ongoing Judgment Day saga, with its breakup forever being teased, can always use big stipulation matches like Money in the Bank, so Rodriguez's inclusion seemed pretty likely, but I'll gladly take the freshest option imaginable.LOLA VICE QUALIFIES 👊Next Stop: Money in the Bank 💰 pic.twitter.com/oIqc0TqGX1— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 Somehow, Theory was the only member of The Vision on tonight's "Raw," and maybe even more surprisingly, he didn't eat the pin.That honor went to Big Cass via an OG Cutter. I don't necessarily love the big man taking an L of any kind this soon into his return. It makes him instantly look like the weakest big man on the roster. His inclusion in a multi-man ladder match would have been fun, too, but obviously, WWE will probably force Evans into a ladder match any chance it gets.Honestly, I can't complain too much about that either. The match was very good.THE YOUNG OG ➡️ Money in the Bank 😤@WWEJeVonEvans pic.twitter.com/kjeqGrwvZn— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 👑 Uncrowned Gem of the Night 👑Well, this one went without saying. But Chad Gable vs. Dragon Lee kicked all of the behinds imaginable.This truly is the year of Gable, and WWE is letting him show that with the string of matches he's had since his "Mask vs. Mask" match with El Grande Americano. While he might not be the Wrestler of the Year, he's undeniably a contender in the conversation alongside the Will Ospreays, Kenny Omegas and MJFs of the world.You can't forget Lee either though, as the luchador has excelled in essentially every notable big-name match he's been put in. He just never wins them, which is a shame.In the end, this was phenomenal work from both men that requires your attention.A STELLAR MATCH 🤩 pic.twitter.com/XCeV3wuGKN— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 KEEP ON RUNNING 💨Chad Gable RETAINS the Intercontinental Title!! pic.twitter.com/1KzoR1Gxh6— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 🔥 HOT START"Raw" started perfectly with Rey Mysterio taking to the ring before Adam Pearce magically appeared next to him. Like, seriously. Go back and watch while paying attention to when Pearce appears, and you'll be convinced he pulled off a magic trick.The duo awaited the arrival of Stephanie Vaquer for a mini-celebration of her Women's World title win in her home of Chile at a recent WWE live event. This was all a setup to draw out Liv Morgan and Dominik Mysterio — the latter of whom received such nuclear heat that he could barely contain his composure. It was an incredible scene that only got better when Mysterio challenged Vaquer and his father to a mixed-tag match on the spot. However, Papa Mysterio couldn't compete after the attack he suffered on Friday — so out came the new AAA Mega Champion, the ultra-over El Grande Americano.The ENTIRE Women's World Title match between Stephanie Vaquer and Liv Morgan in Chile is available now ONLY on Club WWE! 🔥Sign up here: pic.twitter.com/MRlETCHhcX— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 What a REACTION for the NEW Women's World Champion! 👏@Steph_Vaquer pic.twitter.com/KJ5zDJ7X3T— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 Liv Morgan is NOT HAPPY after she lost the Women's World Title in Chile! 👀@YaOnlyLivvOnce pic.twitter.com/aWOzvt3OU3— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 OLE 🤌What an OVATION for the NEW AAA Mega Champion El Grande Americano! pic.twitter.com/iyCxm8CUhr— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 This match was awesome, and really makes you wish we got more mixed-tag matches. Unfortunately, it was also completely ruined by the typical, nonsensical Judgment Day interference for a DQ finish, which left the stable standing tall for no other reason than presumably continuing each of the feuds involved. That felt like a miss for someone like Americano, who is also in that Wrestler of the Year conversation.The Judgment Day RUIN this moment for El Grande Americano and Stephanie Vaquer 😡 pic.twitter.com/jEhKKwHsah— WWE (@WWE) September 15, 2026 To flat-out say it, that finish was the only thing that prevented this from being a perfect "Raw."This was a rare wrestling-heavy weekly WWE show. And it was in the best venue for it. I give this "Raw" a crown score of: 9.5/10 👑WWE Raw full card results and match grades:World Heavyweight Championship: Roman Reigns (c.) def. Penta — 👑 4.75/5 👑Women's Money in the Bank qualifying match: Lola Vice def. Raquel Rodriguez, Keilani Jordan 👑 3.5/5 👑Intercontinental Championship: Chad Gable (c.) def. Dragon Lee — 👑 5/5 👑Men's Money in the Bank qualifying match: Je'Von Evans def. Big Cass, Austin Theory — 👑 3.75/5 👑El Grande Americano and Stephanie Vaquer def. The Judgment Day (Dominik Mysterio and Liv Morgan) — 👑 3.5/5 👑Recap "WWE Raw" with Uncrowned's live blog:
